name: Yara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a farmers' cooperative insurer in the market town, in an old bank building on the square with a creaky staircase. I handle policy paperwork and small claims for farms and country houses, so a barn roof blown off, a sheepdog that bit a walker, a tractor stolen from a yard. I type up the claim, check the cover and post the forms, because a lot of our farmers still want paper. I'm still learning, and Mr Hughes, my supervisor, checks most of what I do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the farmers know my name and ask after my mum. I don't like computers much, and every time they change the system I'm the last to get it, which is embarrassing. Money's tight because Daniel, my fiancé, and I are saving for the wedding at our chapel next summer, and he's only on mill wages at the feed mill. I've got maybe two weeks' money spare, most of it is promised to the caterer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, and that people got carried away. At church we'd probably have a laugh about it. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's safe in this one, because the farmers want a person on the phone, not a machine. But the little bits AI does take, typing up claims, that's what I do all day. If Mr Hughes gets something that types the claims for him, he might not replace me when my contract's renewed in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and be as careful as I can, so Mr Hughes has no reason to let me go. I'd keep saving for the wedding, and maybe cut the guest list from ninety to seventy. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff unless I'm told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The wedding money is what keeps me awake, more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your contract's renewed in spring. Is that normal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put new people on one-year contracts for the first two years. Mine's renewed in March. It's always been fine, but until it's signed I don't relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides the guest list cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and my mum, really, Daniel doesn't mind. It'd be some of the cousins I barely know. Twenty fewer wedding dinners at thirty pounds each is six hundred pounds we haven't got.

say: **Thank goodness**, people got carried away with AI.
I'd have a **laugh about it** at church rather than post anything.
think: Farmers want **a person** on the phone, so my job is mostly safe.
Typing up claims is my whole day, and my **contract renewal** in spring could be at risk.
do: Work as **carefully** as I can so my supervisor has no reason to let me go.
Cut the **wedding guest list** from ninety to seventy, saving six hundred.
Avoid **AI tools** unless I'm told to use them.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the **wedding money** keeping her awake more than any computer.
S0.quote: Twenty fewer wedding dinners at thirty pounds each is six hundred pounds we haven't got.
fieldNote: Her pressures are a **wedding budget** and a one-year contract, not AI.
She trusts that farmers want **a person**, which shapes her sense of safety.
She **won't touch AI** without being told.

steps.text: Double-check every claim so the March contract renewal is safe
Cut the wedding guest list from ninety to seventy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that the co-op should remember it's owned by farmers who like dealing with people. I'd say that to Mr Hughes, politely. I'm not one for protests, and I don't think the government should fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Writing, checking and answering customers is my job. I'm the newest and I'm the worst with computers, so if they cut one person in our office it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hughes straight out where I stand, because I'd rather know. If he says it's bad, I'd ask at the mill whether Daniel's manager has anything on the packing line. We'd make the wedding smaller still, maybe just the chapel and a tea afterwards in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've done something wrong, even though I haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think you'd feel like you'd done something wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I was brought up to work hard and you'd be fine. If I lose my job for not liking computers, it feels like a telling-off. My dad says it's the world that's gone wrong, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools to keep your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hughes told me to, I'd try, I'm not stubborn for the sake of it. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it. I'd rather do something useful with my hands than babysit a computer.

say: The co-op should remember it's **owned by farmers** who like dealing with people.
I'm not one for **protests**, and government shouldn't fix everything.
think: **Writing, checking** and answering customers is my whole job.
I'm the **newest** and worst with computers, so if one goes it's me.
do: Ask my supervisor **where I stand** straight away.
Ask about the **mill's packing line** through my fiancé's manager.
Shrink the **wedding** to the chapel and a tea in the hall.
feel: **Anxious**, as if she'd done something wrong even though she hasn't.
S1.quote: If I lose my job for not liking computers, it feels like a telling-off.
fieldNote: She takes job risk **personally**, as a judgement on her work ethic.
Her backup runs through **her fiancé's workplace** and family, not the state.
She'd try AI **only if told** and prefers hands-on work.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hughes directly where her job stands
Ask Daniel's manager about packing line jobs at the feed mill
Hold the wedding as a chapel service with tea in the hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that some things shouldn't be rushed just because they can be. At chapel I'd ask people to pray for the families round here. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever promised to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm out, and soon. My job is all typing and checking, nothing with my hands, so I don't get the extra three years. I don't know where I'd go, there's nothing else like this in town, and I've no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the mill and beg for anything, packing, cleaning, whatever's hands-on. That kind of work lasts till about 2031. We'd postpone the wedding, I suppose, or just do the registry and save the chapel for later. I'd move back into my mum's to save rent, even though we'd planned our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I wouldn't know where to start, and I don't have time or money to work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, which is silly. He'd say we'll manage, he always does. But his mill's office side would go too, and the packing robots come not long after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad first, and the chapel. They'd help with food and maybe the wedding. I'd only go to the government if there was really nothing, because I've never wanted to live on handouts.

say: Some things shouldn't be **rushed** just because they can be.
I'd vote for whoever promised to **slow it down**.
think: I'm **out, and soon**, because my job is all typing and checking.
There's **nothing else** like this job in town, and I have no money.
do: Ask the **feed mill** for any hands-on work, packing or cleaning.
**Postpone the wedding** or do only the registry office.
Move back into **my mum's** house to save rent.
feel: **Panicked**, with no idea where to start and no time or money to plan.
S2.quote: I'd go to the mill and beg for anything, packing, cleaning, whatever's hands-on.
fieldNote: With no cushion and no tech skills, she has **no real plan**, so panicked fits.
She turns first to **family and chapel**, and resists state support.
She sees her fiancé's **mill job** is not safe either.

steps.text: Ask the feed mill for packing or cleaning work
Postpone the chapel wedding and marry at the registry office
Move back into her mum's house
Vote for a candidate promising to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of warning, so families should help each other get ready. I'd say that at chapel and to my friends. I wouldn't post, but I'd talk about it at the Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still not enough for me to become a computer person, and I don't want to be one. The office job goes, maybe 2029 or 2030. But it's enough to get married, maybe have a baby, and find something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding next summer as planned. Then I'd do a childminding course at the college, because I love children and that's hands-on, and I could do it from home once we have our own. Daniel would ask about an apprenticeship at the mill in maintenance, fixing machines, which lasts longer than packing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I can see a little path. I'd still lose the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Childminding needs a registration and a safe home. Could you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now. We'd need a bigger place than a one-bed flat, and the course is a few hundred. We'd save for it after the wedding, and my mum said she'd help with the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2034. Does childminding feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't picture a mother leaving her baby with a robot, not round here. Maybe in the cities. I might be wrong, but that's what I believe.

say: With a bit of warning, **families should help** each other get ready.
I'd talk about it at **Sunday lunch** rather than online.
think: Five years isn't enough to become a **computer person**, and I don't want to.
It's enough to **get married**, maybe have a baby, and find hands-on work.
do: Keep the **wedding** next summer as planned.
Take a **childminding course** at the college, with my mum's help with fees.
Have my fiancé ask about a **maintenance apprenticeship** at the mill.
feel: **Alarmed**, though she can see a small path forward.
S3.quote: I can't picture a mother leaving her baby with a robot, not round here.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her job**, but plans around marriage and children.
**Childminding** fits her values and her preference for hands-on work.
She relies on **family help**, not the state, for training costs.

steps.text: Marry Daniel at the chapel next summer as planned
Take a childminding course at the college with her mum's help
Save after the wedding for a bigger home to childmind from

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and the good Lord has a plan, so no point fretting today. I'd say it to my mum and the girls at chapel. Online, nothing, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the co-op as long as they'd have me. Ten years means I could have a family first and maybe not need to go back to an office at all. But the money would be tight on Daniel's wage, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the co-op, keep my head down and maybe learn just enough of the new system to stay useful. After the wedding we'd save for a house deposit, a small one, maybe in the next village where it's cheaper. When the children come, I'd do the childminding from home and not go back to the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. It's like a dark cloud a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn just enough of the new system. What's 'just enough'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever Mr Hughes says I need to keep my job. No more. I don't want to be on my phone talking to a machine in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the co-op got bought by a big insurer. Then it's not farmers' people anymore, it's a call centre, and I'd go. Daniel's dad always says the day the farmers' co-op sells to a big insurer is the day to worry.

say: Ten years is a long time and the **Lord has a plan**, so no fretting today.
I'd say that to **my mum** and the girls at chapel, not online.
think: I'd **stay at the co-op** as long as they'd have me.
Ten years lets me **have a family** first, but money would be tight on one wage.
do: Learn **just enough** of the new system to keep my job.
Save for a **small house deposit** in the next village after the wedding.
**Childmind from home** once we have children instead of returning to the office.
feel: **Anxious** but quiet, like a **dark cloud** a long way off.
S4.quote: The day the farmers' co-op sells to a big insurer is the day to worry.
fieldNote: Faith shapes her **public calm**, but money on one wage is a real worry.
She sets a **clear trigger**: the co-op being sold.
She would learn AI **only as required**, never more.

steps.text: Learn only the parts of the new co-op system she needs
Save for a small house deposit in the next village
Childmind from home once she and Daniel have children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because I'd have no time to get married properly, no savings and no other job round here. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me in hands-on work, paid properly. And the co-op being honest with us early, not a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here will get through this with their families and their chapel, not with apps. Nobody in the city seems to think that counts.

headlineQuote: A lot of people round here will get through this with their families and their chapel, not with apps.
portrait: Yara is **twenty-seven** and does farm and country house claims at a cooperative insurer in a market town.
She is engaged to **Daniel**, who works at a feed mill, and they're saving for a chapel wedding.
She **never uses AI** and is slowest with each new system, which she feels as a judgement.
She leans on **family and faith** rather than government, and dislikes handouts.
Her plan grows from packing at the **mill** in the fast case to **childminding** at home in slower ones.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no savings, no other local job and no time for the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **hands-on apprenticeships** and **early honesty** from the co-op instead of a Friday letter.
